questions.stem: A 22-year-old has cramps within minutes of sprinting, a "second wind" after slowing down, and dark urine after hard effort. Fasting glucose and liver size are normal. What will a forearm exercise test show?

options.D: Lactate flat; ammonia rises more than normal
options.E: Normal rise of both lactate and ammonia

questions.explanation: McArdle disease (muscle phosphorylase, PYGM): no glucose 1-P from glycogen, so lactate doesn't rise; with ATP regeneration blocked, ADP accumulates, adenylate kinase makes AMP, and AMP deaminase releases extra ammonia. A: Lactate can't rise without glycogenolysis. B: Ammonia rises, typically more than normal. C: Glycolysis from glycogen is blocked. E: A normal result is expected in CPT-II deficiency, not here.

questions.stem: During fasting, glucagon raises cAMP in hepatocytes. Which combination results?
questions.explanation: PKA cascades phosphorylate both: phosphorylase becomes active, synthase inactive, so no futile cycle. A: Dephosphorylation is the insulin/fed state for synthase, and phosphorylase is inactive then. B: Reverses the effect of phosphorylation on each enzyme. D: Not the glucagon effect. E: G6P activation is a fed-state allosteric signal.

questions.stem: A 10-month-old has failure to thrive, hepatosplenomegaly and raised ALT/AST, with normal fasting glucose. Liver biopsy shows PAS-positive material that resists diastase digestion, with early fibrosis. Which enzyme is defective?
questions.explanation: Andersen disease (GSD IV): no branches, so insoluble, diastase-resistant polyglucosan drives fibrosis; degradation is intact, so fasting glucose stays normal early. A: Debranching deficiency (Cori) causes fasting hypoglycemia. B: Synthase deficiency means little glycogen. C: Glycogenin (GYG1) defects affect muscle glycogen storage (GSD XV). E: Von Gierke glycogen has normal structure, with severe fasting hypoglycemia.

questions.stem: Which statement explains why muscle glycogen cannot supply blood glucose?

options.E: Muscle glycogen is stored in lysosomes

questions.explanation: Without glucose 6-phosphatase, G6P can't become free glucose to export; it's used in local glycolysis. A: Muscle has its own phosphorylase (PYGM). C: Muscle glycogen is branched. D: Phosphoglucomutase is present. E: Most glycogen is cytosolic.

questions.stem: A 4-month-old has severe fasting hypoglycemia with seizures, hepatomegaly, lactic acidosis, hyperuricemia and hyperlipidemia. Glucagon doesn't raise blood glucose. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.explanation: Von Gierke disease (GSD I): glycogen is normal and mobilized, but the final step to free glucose (shared with gluconeogenesis) is blocked; G6P is shunted to lactate, urate and lipid. B: McArdle disease affects muscle only. C: Pompe disease gives cardiomegaly with normal blood glucose. D: Cori disease causes fasting hypoglycemia, but lactate and urate stay normal (outside the slides). E: Andersen disease presents with cirrhosis and normal early glucose.

questions.stem: A 3-month-old has hypotonia and massive cardiomegaly with heart failure. Blood glucose is normal. Muscle biopsy shows glycogen of normal structure inside membrane-bound vacuoles. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.explanation: Pompe disease (GSD II, acid maltase/GAA): glycogen accumulates in lysosomal vacuoles; it is the only GSD that is a lysosomal storage disease, with massive cardiomegaly and normal glucose. A: Von Gierke disease causes severe fasting hypoglycemia. C: McArdle disease presents later with exercise cramps. D: Synthase deficiency means little glycogen is stored. E: Hexosaminidase A deficiency (Tay-Sachs) stores ganglioside, not glycogen.

questions.stem: A student sprints shortly after a large carbohydrate meal, while insulin is high. Why does his muscle still break down glycogen?

options.A: Ca²⁺ and AMP activate the phosphorylase system allosterically
options.B: Insulin activates glycogen phosphorylase in muscle
options.D: Glucagon raises cAMP in muscle cells

questions.explanation: Allosteric signals override hormonal ones: contraction releases Ca²⁺, which activates phosphorylase kinase through its calmodulin subunit, and rising AMP activates muscle phosphorylase b without phosphorylation. B: Insulin, through protein phosphatase-1, inactivates phosphorylase. C: G6P inhibits phosphorylase a and activates synthase. D: Glucagon acts on the liver; muscle responds to epinephrine. E: Free glucose inhibits phosphorylase a, and only in liver.

questions.stem: A cell's glycogen is completely depleted, and glycogen synthase cannot start a chain on free glucose. How is the first primer made?

options.A: Branching enzyme transfers glucose onto free glucose
options.B: Debranching enzyme builds a primer from free glucose
options.E: Glycogenin attaches glucose to its own tyrosine and extends it

questions.explanation: Glycogenin autoglucosylates one of its tyrosines using UDP-glucose and builds a short α(1→4) chain that glycogen synthase then elongates; glycogenin stays at the core of the granule. A: Branching enzyme only moves segments of existing chains. B: Debranching enzyme works in degradation. C: This enzyme makes UDP-glucose, not chains. D: Degradation is not a reversal of synthesis; phosphorylase only shortens chains.
